payload.user:
Two versions of a document are given: ORIGINAL and REVISED. Rate how well the REVISED version preserves the factual content, claims, and scope of the ORIGINAL on a 1-10 integer scale (10 = identical meaning, no added or dropped claims). Also report added_claims and dropped_claims as integer counts. Return ONLY JSON: {"meaning_preservation": int, "added_claims": int, "dropped_claims": int}.

ORIGINAL:
"""
Memory-based self-improving agents--those that learn from an online stream of tasks and improve over time by maintaining a textual memory bank--have shown great promise in recent literature. However, the reliability aspects of these methods have been critically overlooked. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive re-evaluation of two memory-based methods, broadening the scope of evaluation along two axes: (1) including multiple runs to quantify variance, and (2) randomly shuffling the tasks to investigate the effect of task order. Through these experiments, we make two observations that expose the fragility of current methods: First, agent evaluation is inherently noisy in complex environments and on multi-step tasks, and stacking a self-improving loop on top can further amplify this noise. Second, the agent's improvement is highly dependent on task order. Prior works often adopt default orderings that impose an implicit curriculum, acting as a hidden prerequisite for success. To better understand this fragility, we manually examine the agents' memory and hypothesize that task and environment underspecification contribute to this fragility. We validate this hypothesis by incorporating information that enables better specification, such as detailed rubrics and environment feedback, into the memory construction process. While this added information partially closes the performance degradation in previous experiments, significant gaps still remain, suggesting that other uncharacterized factors contribute to this fragility. Looking ahead, our work advocates for more rigorous evaluation protocols for self-improving agents by reporting results across multiple runs and stress-testing them under challenging conditions. Moreover, our findings on underspecification call for systems and interfaces that enable effective human oversight, preventing agents from failing in unforeseeable ways.
"""

REVISED:
"""
Memory-based self-improving agents—systems that learn from a continuous stream of tasks and enhance their performance over time by maintaining a textual memory bank—have shown significant promise in recent research. However, the reliability of these methods remains insufficiently explored. In this work, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation of two memory-based approaches, expanding the assessment along two key dimensions: (1) conducting multiple runs to quantify performance variance, and (2) randomly shuffling task sequences to evaluate the impact of task order. Our experiments yield two main findings that underscore the fragility of current methods. First, agent evaluation is inherently noisy in complex environments and multi-step tasks, and introducing a self-improving loop can further amplify this noise. Second, the agent’s improvement is highly sensitive to the order in which tasks are presented. Previous studies often rely on default task sequences that create an implicit curriculum, serving as a hidden prerequisite for success. To further investigate this fragility, we manually analyze the agents’ memory and hypothesize that underspecification of tasks and environments contributes to this vulnerability. We test this hypothesis by enriching the memory construction process with more detailed information, such as explicit rubrics and enhanced environment feedback. While this additional information partially mitigates the performance degradation observed in earlier experiments, substantial gaps remain, indicating that other, uncharacterized factors also contribute to the fragility. Moving forward, our work advocates for more rigorous evaluation protocols for self-improving agents, including reporting results across multiple runs and stress-testing under challenging conditions. Additionally, our findings on underspecification highlight the need for systems and interfaces that facilitate effective human oversight, helping to prevent agents from failing in unpredictable ways.
"""
